What GuildOS is
GuildOS is a community, event, and career platform for students, campus organizations, and professional communities.
It connects community membership, events, attendance, projects, leadership, certificates, and career opportunities.
Its central purpose is to help people organize activities, record participation, and turn those activities into a credible track record.
Who the website serves
Students and members: discover communities, attend events, build projects, earn certificates, and find opportunities.
Community organizers: manage members, leadership, events, attendance, finances, and records.
Schools and institutions: gain a clearer record of community activities and student involvement.
Sponsors: discover events to support and review delivery reports.
Recruiters: publish opportunities and discover candidates using their profiles and recorded achievements.
Platform administrators: oversee verification, moderation, payments, and access.
Community creation and management
Organizations can create a community page with their identity, description, interests, and contact information.
Students can discover, follow, and join communities.
Organizers can handle membership requests and manage existing members.
Different leadership roles provide different permissions.
Communities can connect their existing WhatsApp, Discord, Telegram, Slack, or other community spaces.
This allows GuildOS to work alongside the platforms a community already uses.
Unverified communities have a restricted set of capabilities until verification is completed.
Community Mode and organizer access
Student participation and organizer access are separate.
Community Mode requires personal approval before protected organizer tools become available.
Approval alone does not give someone control over another community; they also need the appropriate active membership and role.
Removed or suspended members should not retain management authority through an old role.
A community’s verification status is separate from an individual organizer’s approval.
Sensitive features, including certificates and paid-event capabilities, retain their additional verification requirements.
Leadership records and succession
Communities can maintain leadership rosters for different academic sessions or terms.
They can record names, positions, and service periods.
Leadership lists can be imported from supported documents for review.
Outgoing leadership can be recorded as past leadership.
Organizers can hand responsibilities to incoming leaders and transfer ownership where appropriate.
Eligible leadership service can receive verifiable certificates and contribute to the member’s record.
This helps a community retain its history when executives graduate or leave.
Event planning and publishing
Organizers can create workshops, seminars, meetups, hackathons, and other events.
Events can be physical, online, or hybrid.
Event pages can include descriptions, schedules, venues, speakers, volunteers, partners, and sponsors.
Registration can support capacity limits, approval requirements, invitations, and waitlists.
Organizers can collect event-specific registration answers.
Multi-day events can have separate daily schedules and attendance requirements.
Parallel sections or tracks can have their own venues, trainers, and capacity.
Previous events can be copied into new drafts to reduce repeated setup work.
Events can be postponed, rescheduled, or canceled through the relevant organizer flows.
Student event discovery and registration
Students can browse events and filter them by relevant categories, location, format, and other available options.
They can save events and add them to their calendars.
GuildOS keeps their account identity available across events, reducing repeated profile entry.
Each event still has its own registration and eligibility requirements.
A confirmed registration that stays on GuildOS displays a success popup.
Its Discover more events button prioritizes similar topics and event types.
Waitlisted and approval-pending students receive the appropriate pending status instead of a confirmed-registration message.
Support for events hosted on other platforms
Communities can continue using an external registration platform required by a company, school, or parent organization.
An organizer can paste a public event link and preview details extracted from that page.
Extracted information must be reviewed before saving.
GuildOS can save the student’s registration and direct them to the official external registration page.
Students are encouraged to use their GuildOS email on that external site.
A Copy email button makes this easier.
Students who used another email can expand the alternate-email option and verify ownership of that address.
Organizers can import registration and attendance reports, with records matched against verified member emails.
Unmatched records remain available for review and rechecking.
Clear external-registration statuses
GuildOS distinguishes a student opening the external page, a student reporting that they completed registration, and registration matched against an organizer’s report.
Opening a link does not prove registration was completed.
Verifying another email proves ownership of that email; it does not prove event registration or attendance.
Direct confirmation through external-platform APIs or webhooks is not included in the current external-event flow.
Attendance recording
GuildOS-managed events support check-in and check-out workflows, including QR-based attendance.
Online events have their relevant joining and attendance flows.
Multi-day events can track attendance separately for each day.
Certificate eligibility can consider attendance duration and required days.
Events using external attendance reports do not require students to repeat check-in and check-out in GuildOS.
Organizers can review attendance records and import supported CSV or TSV reports.
Matching uses verified emails rather than guessing from names.
Import rules help prevent duplicate duration counting and inappropriate changes to existing attendance or issued certificates.
Public event transparency
Event pages show confirmed registration totals.
Attendance totals remain pending until the event has ended and attendance is finalized.
Finalized totals distinguish attendance from registration.
Attendance sources are labeled, including GuildOS check-in and organizer-uploaded reports.
Public totals provide visibility without exposing attendee email lists.
Private-event access restrictions still apply.
These figures help students and sponsors assess participation, while the source labels explain the evidence behind them.
Certificates and verification
Eligible participants can receive certificates linked to their recorded activity.
Certificates have unique serial numbers and QR verification links.
Anyone receiving a certificate link can check its corresponding GuildOS record.
Organizers have certificate templates and customization tools.
Depending on the available entitlement, customization can include wording, colors, fonts, signatures, and other design elements.
Certificates can include relevant community, partner, or sponsor branding.
The platform supports attendance, leadership, and hackathon-related certificate flows.
Organizer-imported attendance remains labeled as organizer-reported evidence.
Certificate verification confirms the recorded credential; it does not independently authenticate the origin of an uploaded spreadsheet.
Hackathon management
Participants can create or join teams.
Teams can submit project descriptions, repository links, demos, videos, images, and technology information.
Organizers can configure tracks and judging criteria.
Invited judges can review and score submissions through their judging pages.
Organizers can review every submitted project from their dashboard.
Organizers choose and publish the winners.
The public hackathon page shows winning projects only after results are published.
Teams retain private access to their own submissions.
Winning projects can be saved to the community’s Knowledge Hub.
Eligible participants and winners can receive the relevant achievements and certificates.
Guild Score and member reputation
Guild Score records contributions across supported activities.
These can include attendance, leadership, organizing, speaking, volunteering, hackathon work, and knowledge contributions.
The score has an activity ledger so members can understand where points came from.
Verification and eligibility rules determine which activities qualify.
It helps make consistent participation and contribution more visible.
Guild Score is an activity-based reputation signal; it is not a complete measure of someone’s ability or employability.
Profiles, portfolios, and CVs
Members can maintain profiles showing their interests, skills, communities, and achievements.
Recorded certificates, leadership, and project activity can support their public professional identity.
The CV builder can assemble information from their GuildOS history.
AI assistance can help improve presentation and wording.
Public CV verification links let others compare supported claims with platform records.
Users can refresh a CV when their activity record changes.
External credentials can be added but remain distinguished from GuildOS-verified records.
This helps students build evidence of involvement alongside their academic qualifications.
Opportunities and recruitment
Students can discover opportunities and record actions such as saving, expressing interest, or applying.
Matching can use relevant profile information and platform activity.
Recruiters have a dedicated portal for publishing and managing opportunities.
Recruiters can review candidates and move them through an applicant pipeline.
Candidate discovery supports filters such as institution, department, leadership, reputation, and availability.
Recruiter verification and opportunity moderation provide additional trust signals.
Recruiters can view analytics for their listings and candidate activity.
These tools support discovery and review; they do not guarantee selection or employment.
Sponsorship
Organizations and brands can discover events seeking sponsorship.
Sponsors can submit inquiries or offers.
Organizers can manage discussions and record sponsorship agreements and deliverables.
Supported sponsorships can be paid through GuildOS.
Relevant branding can appear on event pages, certificates, and thank-you content.
Sponsor reports can show participation figures, attendance evidence, and feedback.
Reports distinguish GuildOS-recorded attendance from organizer-uploaded attendance.
This gives sponsors a more structured way to evaluate what an event delivered.
Paid tickets and organizer finances
Verified, eligible communities can run paid events.
Ticketing supports features such as tiers, promotional codes, group purchases, and discounts.
Group purchases can provide individual claim links for attendees.
Organizers can review sales and their community wallet.
Payout and refund workflows support the financial side of events.
Supported payment providers include Paystack and Flutterwave.
Actual availability depends on the configured provider, community eligibility, and platform settings.
Platform revenue can come from ticket commissions, sponsorship fees, and premium customization.
Communication and engagement
Members and communities can publish posts and updates.
Feeds support engagement through comments, reactions, and polls.
Communities can publish announcements.
Notifications help members follow registrations, events, certificates, and other relevant activity.
Messaging and connection features help members maintain relationships.
Sharing event and achievement links helps communities reach more people.
Post-event feedback helps organizers understand attendee experiences.
Knowledge Hub and AI assistance
Communities can preserve articles, links, files, guides, and useful resources.
This helps retain institutional knowledge across leadership changes.
Members can discover relevant knowledge through search.
The assistant can use supported community resources, event information, and the member’s accessible records.
AI tools also support areas such as CV wording, event planning, and feedback summaries.
AI output still needs judgment and review, especially when importing or drafting information.
Advantages for students
One place to discover communities, events, projects, and opportunities.
Less repeated profile entry.
Easier access to personal event records and certificates.
A clearer history of participation and leadership.
More evidence to support a CV or portfolio.
A way to recover report matches when an external platform uses another email.
Opportunities to gain visibility through contributions beyond exam results.
Advantages for organizers and institutions
Fewer disconnected spreadsheets and manual certificate processes.
Membership, leadership, events, attendance, and reporting connected in one platform.
Continued use of existing chat communities and required external event platforms.
Better continuity when leadership changes.
More structured sponsor communication and reporting.
Clearer permission boundaries for community management.
A distinction between registration numbers, actual attendance, and the source of attendance evidence.
What makes GuildOS distinctive
Its value comes from connecting the full journey: community → event → participation → achievement → profile → opportunity.
Event activity remains useful after the event ends.
Community leadership becomes part of a lasting record.
External-platform support reduces the need for organizations to abandon their existing tools.
Evidence labels make the strength and origin of a record clearer.
It brings organizer operations and student development into the same system.
Current limits and important boundaries
External registration cannot be confirmed merely by decoding or opening a link.
Event-link extraction depends on what the source website makes publicly accessible.
Uploaded reports remain organizer-reported evidence.
Some mismatches require verification and organizer review.
Email, payment, storage, and AI features depend on their configured services.
The native mobile app is still at an early stage.
The platform improves traceability and accountability, but it cannot eliminate every false claim or form of attendance fraud.
